finding.shortLabel: Earsham testator and his minor son are both the wrong generation to be the emigrant
finding.statement: The Earsham testator died in 1638 and his son John was still a minor at that date (born after about 1624), so neither man is the Massachusetts emigrant, who was already at Weymouth by June 1641 and had married his own wife Mary well before 1628. What the will documents instead is a previously unlogged Waveney-valley Gurney yeoman family, distinctive enough -- the rare brother's forename, a dead brother's four named sons -- to recognize and set aside wherever it resurfaces. This family's own further history, traced forward through a 1710 Bungay nuncupative will, a 1690s Bungay merchant's will naming Sarah Gurney's children, and an eighteenth-century Earsham manorial court book, is carried on its own dedicated subject file rather than in this graph.

finding.shortLabel: 1638 Earsham will: testator, wife Mary, son John a minor at fourteen, brother Syon/Lyon

sources.locator: Registered copy will, p. 168 of the Norwich-circuit will register, FamilySearch film 008076858, images 454-455; proved Norwich 26 Dec 1639

finding.statement: John Gurney of Earsham ('Eursham'), Norfolk, yeoman, made his will on 10 August 1638, sick in body, holding messuages, lands, and tenements at Earsham both freehold and copyhold. His wife, Mary, was to hold the estate during their son's minority, then take a 4-pound annual annuity in lieu of dower. Their son, John, a minor, takes the whole estate at fourteen; if he died before twenty-one the estate passed instead to the testator's brother, named in the will's own text as 'Lyon Gurney' but read on a closer paleographic pass as Syon -- the same forename, and the same misreading trap, recurring across this family's later records. A second brother, Robert Gurney, was already dead by 1638, leaving four sons (including a William and a Robert) 5-pound legacies apiece; a brother-in-law, John Youngman of St Andrew's, served as co-executor alongside Syon. The will was proved at Norwich on 26 December 1639.
